checkpoints: Don't take the team's verbal confirmation at face value — first decode the actual JWT used in this run (e.g. `echo $ID_TOKEN | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d | jq`) to see the real `aud`, `sub`, `iss` for this specific run, instead of guessing or trusting a description.

The prime suspect: the `sub` claim's format differs by execution context — a workflow running directly on a branch yields `repo:org/repo:ref:refs/heads/main`, while one using `environment: prod` yields `repo:org/repo:environment:prod` instead; the team's "confirmed correct for main" may only hold for the branch-ref format, so if the deploy job actually runs under an `environment`, the real `sub` sent won't match that trust-policy condition and STS will reject it — even though it logically "is" the main branch.
If `sub` turns out not to match, fix the trust policy by using `StringLike` with a pattern covering the actual `sub` format, or by adding a separate condition for the `environment`.
If `sub` does match, next rule out whether `aud` is exactly `sts.amazonaws.com` — an audience mismatch means a token minted for a different service can't be reused to assume the AWS role.
Also verify the workflow declares `permissions: id-token: write` — without it, GitHub never issues the OIDC token in the first place.

As a rarer, later-order possibility, check whether the OIDC provider's thumbprint is stale — generally no longer an issue since AWS switched to CA-root verification in 2023, but still worth ruling out for an older provider.

Directly calling kms:Encrypt on the 500MB file is infeasible because AWS KMS Encrypt has a hard payload limit of 4KB per call, and 500MB is hundreds of thousands of times beyond that limit, so the API would reject it outright.
The correct model is envelope encryption, which uses an outer KEK (key encryption key) — the actual CMK living inside KMS/HSM — that never leaves KMS in plaintext form.
The inner layer is a DEK (data key) — a symmetric key freshly generated for each encryption operation, used to actually encrypt the data.

The encrypt flow starts by calling kms:GenerateDataKey, which returns two copies of the DEK: a plaintext copy (used immediately then discarded) and a KEK-encrypted copy that is only a few hundred bytes and safe to store.
The plaintext DEK is used to encrypt the 500MB file entirely locally, never going back through KMS, because local symmetric encryption is fast and has no size limit.
After encrypting, the plaintext DEK is discarded from memory, keeping only the encrypted data plus its accompanying encrypted DEK.
The decrypt flow is symmetric: only the encrypted DEK (small, under 4KB) is sent through kms:Decrypt to recover the plaintext DEK, which is then used to decrypt the 500MB file locally.
The key point is that the KEK inside KMS/HSM never sees the real data — it only encrypts/decrypts one tiny DEK at a time, while encrypting the large data blob happens entirely locally.

Không coi việc Pod vẫn chạy ổn là tín hiệu an toàn — phải thận trọng vì lý do kỹ thuật cụ thể: ESO duy trì K8s Secret theo mô hình last-known-good, khi sync lỗi thì Secret hiện tại (cũ) vẫn được giữ nguyên nên Pod vẫn chạy được, chứ không phải vì mọi thứ đang ổn.

Bước điều tra đầu tiên: chạy `kubectl describe externalsecret checkout-db-creds -n checkout` và đọc `status.conditions` để biết loại lỗi cụ thể (ví dụ ResourceNotFoundException, AccessDenied) thay vì đoán mò.

Giả thuyết 1: `remoteRef.key` (`prod/checkout/db-password`) không còn khớp tên secret thật trên AWS Secrets Manager, có thể do ai đó đã đổi tên/xóa secret cũ rồi tạo secret mới; xác minh bằng `aws secretsmanager describe-secret --secret-id prod/checkout/db-password`, lỗi 404 sẽ xác nhận giả thuyết này.

Giả thuyết 2: ServiceAccount của ESO controller (qua IRSA) đã mất quyền `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue`, có thể do ai đó sửa IAM policy hoặc trust relationship của role gắn với ServiceAccount; xác minh bằng cách assume đúng role đó rồi thử gọi trực tiếp `GetSecretValue` để biết quyền còn hay mất.

Đây là con dao hai lưỡi: nếu lỗi sync trùng đúng lúc secret bị rotate thật trên AWS (ví dụ DBA đổi mật khẩu database), Pod sẽ tiếp tục dùng credential cũ đã bị vô hiệu hóa ở nguồn cho tới khi được restart hoặc sync phục hồi, tạo thành sự cố kép: vừa mất khả năng lấy secret mới, vừa có thể gặp lỗi xác thực database bất cứ lúc nào mà không có cảnh báo trước.

Với `refreshInterval: 1h`, độ trễ phát hiện sự cố có thể lên tới một giờ nếu chỉ dựa vào việc chờ Pod bị lỗi mới biết; do đó nhóm nên chủ động giám sát metric `externalsecret_sync_calls_error` thay vì chờ triệu chứng xảy ra.

Root cause: KV v2 stores actual data at the real API path `<mount>/data/<key>` (metadata separately at `<mount>/metadata/<key>`) — the `data/` prefix is how the engine separates the data API from the metadata API.

The current policy `path "secret/checkout/*"` only matches `/v1/secret/checkout/*`, NOT `/v1/secret/data/checkout/*`, which is the actual path the app's request hits — this mismatch is why Vault returns `403 permission denied`.

Why the coworker's test was misleading: the `vault kv get` CLI command automatically inserts the `data/` prefix under the hood — typing `secret/checkout/db` actually calls `GET /v1/secret/data/checkout/db`, not the literal path shown.

The CLI test succeeding proves nothing about the checkout service's own policy: it ran under the coworker's own token, which may have broader or different permissions than the service's AppRole-issued token — so a passing CLI call doesn't validate what the service's policy actually grants.
Fix: change the policy to `path "secret/data/checkout/*" { capabilities = ["read", "list"] }`.

If the service also needs version history for rollback, add a separate `path "secret/metadata/checkout/*" { capabilities = ["read", "list"] }` block, since metadata is a completely different KV v2 API path not automatically covered by data-read permission.

To verify correctly instead of trusting the coworker's CLI test, use `vault kv get -output-policy secret/checkout/db` (Vault prints the exact required policy path) or call the HTTP API directly with `curl` using the service's own token to reproduce the actual 403.

Root cause — non-idempotent statement: `revocation_statements` lacks `IF EXISTS`, so when a transient error occurs after `DROP ROLE` has already succeeded, Vault's retry mechanism re-issues the same `DROP ROLE` call and now hits a genuine PostgreSQL error ("role does not exist").

Consequence: Vault cannot distinguish an already-completed revoke from a real failure on that error, so the lease/role state ends up stuck or unresolved in Vault's tracking even though the role is already gone from PostgreSQL.

Core fix: rewrite the statement to `DROP ROLE IF EXISTS "{{name}}";` so a retry after the role is already deleted returns success instead of an error — making revocation idempotent no matter how many times Vault calls it.

Second accumulation source: `DROP ROLE` can also fail (and leave the role behind) if it still owns objects like tables/sequences, or has an active session/connection open, causing PostgreSQL to refuse deletion with a "role still has dependencies" error.

Fix for the dependency/ownership issue: prepend `REASSIGN OWNED BY "{{name}}" TO someadmin; DROP OWNED BY "{{name}}";` before the `DROP ROLE IF EXISTS` line so all bindings are cleared before the role is dropped.
This config fix alone won't retroactively clean up roles already accumulated, so run a periodic query to find `v-app-%` roles no longer tracked by Vault and remove them.
For leases Vault still holds where the database-side revoke keeps failing, use `vault lease revoke --force` to force Vault to clean up its own tracking independent of the database execution result.
Identifies the core problem: every service calls AWS KMS's kms:Encrypt/kms:Decrypt directly, hard-wiring encryption logic to one specific cloud vendor's API with no shared abstraction layer.
States that AWS KMS ciphertext is not compatible with GCP Cloud KMS — data encrypted by AWS KMS cannot simply be decrypted using a GCP key.

Names at least one concrete downside of the current design for the GCP move: either a costly/risky re-encryption of all existing data, or permanently running two parallel encryption systems that are hard to audit consistently.
Proposes the redesign direction of inserting an abstraction/encryption-service layer between services and the cloud KMS, so switching providers doesn't require changing each service's code.
Proposes SOPS (or an equivalent client-side tool) as one option, noting its backend is pluggable/swappable (e.g. age/AWS KMS/GCP KMS/Vault) while the file format and service code stay the same.
Proposes HashiCorp Vault Transit (or an equivalent self-hosted encryption service) as an option that exposes a KMS-like encrypt/decrypt API but can run on any infrastructure.
Reasons that only the self-hosted option (e.g. Vault) can satisfy the future on-premise/compliance requirement, because AWS KMS is inherently tied to AWS and can never be run on-premise.

Mentions envelope encryption (KEK wrapping a small DEK that encrypts the bulk data) as the reason a KMS migration can be low-disruption — only the small DEK needs re-encrypting, not the already-encrypted bulk data.
Trust policy dùng Principal.Federated trỏ đúng ARN của IAM OIDC provider đã đăng ký cho GitHub (token.actions.githubusercontent.com) — không phải ARN của provider khác hay role ARN thường.

Action phải là sts:AssumeRoleWithWebIdentity (KHÔNG phải sts:AssumeRole) vì đây là external IdP flow: token do GitHub OIDC cấp cho caller chưa có sẵn AWS credentials, khác với AssumeRole vốn dùng cho caller đã có credentials AWS sẵn.
Điều kiện aud dùng StringEquals với giá trị chính xác "sts.amazonaws.com" — chặn được mọi token được mint cho audience khác (vd GCP) tái sử dụng để assume role AWS này, thoả yêu cầu (3).

Điều kiện sub dùng StringEquals (KHÔNG phải StringLike với wildcard) với chuỗi CHÍNH XÁC "repo:StarCi-Academy/orders-service:ref:refs/heads/main" — chỉ khớp đúng một repo, một branch, thoả yêu cầu (1).

Một phiên bản "trông có vẻ đúng" nhưng SAI dùng StringLike với sub "repo:StarCi-Academy/*:*" là anti-pattern nghiêm trọng: wildcard đầu cho phép MỌI repo trong org (không chỉ orders-service) assume role, wildcard sau cho phép MỌI ref (mọi branch, mọi PR, mọi tag) — vi phạm trực tiếp cả yêu cầu (1) lẫn tinh thần yêu cầu (2).

Yêu cầu (2) chặn fork PR được đảm bảo GIÁN TIẾP nhờ chính việc match sub chính xác: workflow chạy từ pull_request của fork có sub chứa tên/owner của FORK đó (khác với StarCi-Academy/orders-service), nên tự động không khớp điều kiện mà không cần logic "block fork" riêng.

Lớp phòng thủ thứ hai nằm ở phía workflow (không phải trust policy): GitHub mặc định KHÔNG cấp quyền id-token: write cho workflow được trigger bởi pull_request từ fork, nên trong đa số trường hợp token thậm chí không được cấp phát — hai lớp này cùng nhau tạo độ chắc chắn thực sự.

Core difference is about who gets to create provenance and where: Level 2 only requires provenance to be signed by a hosted build platform, but the main build job itself can still generate and sign its own provenance (self-attestation).
This L2 gap means an attacker who compromises the main build job can forge provenance claiming "I built cleanly."
Level 3 requires the build environment to be ephemeral (not reused across builds, so no state leaks from one build to the next).
Level 3 requires provenance to be generated by the build platform in a separate, isolated job that the main build job cannot read from or write to.
This isolation requirement is why slsa-github-generator always runs two independent jobs — build and provenance — rather than one job doing both.
Tie to SolarWinds: the 2020 attacker compromised the internal build pipeline (not the source code), and the shipped binary still had a valid signature because the build system itself signed it.
L3 doesn't eliminate the risk entirely — if the GitHub Actions runner infrastructure itself were compromised, provenance could still be forged.
L3's real value is raising attack cost: it forces the attacker to compromise large-scale, heavily-audited build platform infrastructure instead of a lightly-watched internal build server.

Deploy manifest must reference the image by an immutable digest (`image: repo/app@sha256:digest`) rather than a mutable tag like `:latest`/`:v1`, since a tag is just a pointer that can be redirected to different content later while a digest pins the exact content.

Policy Controller (the cluster's admission webhook) verifies the cosign signature at Pod-creation time and denies any request to run an image without a valid signature before it ever reaches etcd; because this check runs at the API-server/cluster level rather than inside CI, it still catches an unsigned image even if someone bypasses CI entirely and pushes directly to the registry.

Admission control only verifies ONCE, at the moment the Pod is created — it does not continuously re-check an image that is already running, so it cannot by itself detect a registry compromise that happens after deployment.

To catch a post-deploy image swap, you need periodic re-verification — running `cosign verify` on a schedule (e.g., a CronJob) or integrating it into a scanner like Trivy — to re-audit the currently running image.

The real guarantee comes from combining all three layers together: digest pinning blocks a swapped tag, admission control blocks an unsigned image at deploy time, and periodic verification catches a post-deploy swap; relying on only one or two layers leaves a gap.
Overall verdict: despite looking like it has enough steps, this CI gate blocks almost nothing.
Trivy is never passed `--exit-code 1`, so by default it exits 0 even when it finds CRITICAL findings — the step only prints CVEs to the log instead of ever signaling failure.
Even if Trivy did exit non-zero, `allow_failure: true` on the job would let the pipeline pass anyway — a second, independent reason the step can't act as a gate.

The SBOM is generated from `$BASE_IMAGE` (the image before the Dockerfile's `RUN` steps install app dependencies), so it's missing every app-layer library and the scan barely covers the base OS, missing exactly the code you wrote — the SBOM must instead be generated from the FINAL image (the one actually built and pushed, after all install steps).

There's no vulnerability-database-update step (e.g. `trivy image --download-db-only`) before scanning, so if the runner caches a stale DB, Trivy will miss a CVE published just yesterday for a dependency that's been sitting in the image for a while — a "clean" scan today means nothing if the DB isn't fresh.

There's no VEX mechanism for handling false positives: when a genuinely non-exploitable CVE shows up, without VEX the only remaining options are lowering the severity threshold (losing the ability to catch real CVEs) or dropping the gate entirely — both worse than justifying each CVE with evidence via VEX.
